snapshots.name: Faust
snapshots.body: The scholar who has read everything and knows nothing worth knowing, and signs away his soul for one moment he would want to keep. The wager is his own idea, and so is its wording.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mephistopheles
snapshots.body: The devil who bets the Lord that he can have Faust, and then finds that ruining him is harder than it looked. He calls himself the spirit that always denies, and he is the funniest thing in the play.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Margaret
snapshots.body: Gretchen: a girl of fourteen or fifteen who has never been outside her own street. What Faust does to her is the whole second half of the play, and the last word on her is not his.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Lord
snapshots.body: God in the Prologue in Heaven, who lets Mephistopheles have his wager because a man’s striving needs a companion who goads.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Spirit of the Earth
snapshots.body: The power Faust conjures and cannot bear to look at, which tells him he resembles the spirit he can grasp — and not this one.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Martha
snapshots.body: Margaret’s neighbour, a widow who is not much troubled about her missing husband and is very ready to be courted by Mephistopheles.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Valentine
snapshots.body: Margaret’s brother, a soldier, who used to be proud of her name and dies in the street outside her door cursing it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Bessy
snapshots.body: The neighbour at the well who tells Margaret, with relish, what has happened to Barbara — not knowing she is describing Margaret’s own future.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Evil Spirit
snapshots.body: The voice behind Margaret in the cathedral, which asks her how things stood when she was still innocent.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Barbara
snapshots.body: The girl in the next street who was got with child and abandoned; Bessy tells the story to Margaret without seeing what it means.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Agatha
snapshots.body: A girl at the city gate, called away by her friend so as not to be seen with fortune-tellers.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Catherine
snapshots.body: The girl in Mephistopheles’s serenade under Margaret’s window, warned not to go in to her lover as a maiden.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The King in Thule
snapshots.body: The faithful king of the song Margaret sings while she undresses, who kept his dead love’s golden cup until he died.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Mater Dolorosa
snapshots.body: The image of the Virgin in the wall of the Zwinger, with flowers before it, that Margaret prays to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Wagner
snapshots.body: Faust’s assistant, entirely content with books and eager to be told he is making progress. Goethe uses him to show what Faust might have settled for.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Student
snapshots.body: The freshman who comes for advice and is sent off by Mephistopheles, in Faust’s gown, with a course of study designed to ruin him — and an autograph that reads "you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil."
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Poodle
snapshots.body: The black dog that follows Faust home from the walk and turns out to be the devil; Faust spends a whole scene talking to it before it changes shape.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Nostradamus
snapshots.body: The astrologer whose book of signs Faust opens, and in which he finds the sign of the Macrocosm and then the sign of the Earth Spirit.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Frosch
snapshots.body: One of the four drinkers in Auerbach’s Cellar, and the one who tries hardest to keep the party going.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Brander
snapshots.body: A drinker in Auerbach’s Cellar, who sings the song about the rat that ate poison.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Siebel
snapshots.body: A drinker in Auerbach’s Cellar, unlucky in love and the first to grab for Mephistopheles’s throat.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Altmayer
snapshots.body: The fourth drinker in Auerbach’s Cellar, and the soberest of them.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Witch
snapshots.body: The keeper of the kitchen where Faust is made thirty years younger; she recognises Mephistopheles at once and is scolded for using his old names.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Monkeys
snapshots.body: The witch’s household, who mind the cauldron, play with a crown and a glass ball, and beg for money.

snapshots.name: Helen

snapshots.body: Named by Mephistopheles for what the philtre will do.

snapshots.body: The first of the three archangels in the Prologue in Heaven, who sings of the sun and its brother spheres.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.body: The second archangel of the Prologue, who sings of the earth turning between splendour and night.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.body: In the Prelude on the Stage, the one who wants a full house and tells the Poet what an audience actually is.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Merryman

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The townsfolk at the gate
snapshots.body: Goethe’s crowd on Easter Sunday, speaking in anonymous voices — mechanics choosing a tavern, servant-girls, burghers glad of a war far away in Turkey, a beggar, a soldier, a citizen’s daughter warned off the fortune-teller. None of them is named, and that is the point: this is the world Faust cannot be content with.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Old Peasant
snapshots.body: The villager who brings Faust the first draught, because Faust’s father worked among them in the plague year — the thanks that makes Faust confess what his father’s medicine actually did.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Faust’s father
snapshots.body: The dark man of honour who brewed the red lion and the lily in his laboratory and killed more patients than the plague; Faust says so while accepting their gratitude.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Luther
snapshots.body: Named only for his paunch, in Brander’s song about the rat.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr Hans of Rippach
snapshots.body: A stock joke — the man from Rippach who does not exist, whom Mephistopheles is asked whether he supped with.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jack Rake
snapshots.body: The name Margaret’s type of admirer is given: a man who covets every flower for himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Will-o’-the-Wisp
snapshots.body: The zigzag light pressed into service as a guide up the Brocken, and told to go straight for once.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Lilith
snapshots.body: Adam’s first wife, dancing on the Brocken; Mephistopheles warns Faust about her beautiful hair.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Squire Voland
snapshots.body: The old German name for the devil, which Mephistopheles uses to clear a path through the crowd on the mountain.

snapshots.name: The General

snapshots.body: Goethe’s caricature of a living critic who denied ghosts in print; he turns up on a mountain full of them and complains that they will not obey the rules.

snapshots.name: Titania

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Puck
snapshots.body: Shakespeare’s sprite, come whirling into the masque.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Ariel
snapshots.body: The airy spirit of The Tempest, leading the song in the masque.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Herald
snapshots.body: Who announces the golden wedding of Oberon and Titania.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Orchestra
snapshots.body: The band of gnats, flies and frogs that accompanies the masque, tuning up and signing off.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.body: A single voice in the masque’s chorus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Spirit that is Fashioning Itself
snapshots.body: A half-made creature in the masque, all legs and no body yet.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: A Pair of Lovers
snapshots.body: Two figures slipping away from the masque into the dark.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Inquisitive Traveller
snapshots.body: The tourist who asks whether all this is masquerade, and recognises Oberon.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Orthodox
snapshots.body: Who sees no claws and no tail and concludes that, like the gods of Greece, this one is a devil too.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.body: The literary pedant who objects that the witches are not delicately enough drawn.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Young Witch
snapshots.body: Who says dress and paint are for the old, and rides naked.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Matron
snapshots.body: Who is too well-bred to quarrel, and hopes the young one rots.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Leader of the Band
snapshots.body: Who tries to keep the insects off the naked witch.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Weathercock
snapshots.body: Who faces one way and then the other in two consecutive speeches — Goethe’s joke about turncoats.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Xenien
snapshots.body: The stinging epigrams Goethe and Schiller had published together, appearing in the masque as insects.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.body: A journalist who had attacked the Xenien; he appears here as one of the pests.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Musaget
snapshots.body: The name of Hennings’s journal, personified as a leader of muses who would rather lead witches.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Ci-devant Genius of the Age
snapshots.body: Another of Hennings’s journals, which claims the Brocken as the German Parnassus.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Crane
snapshots.body: Lavater, the physiognomist, who fishes in clear water and in muddy.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Worldling
snapshots.body: Who observes that the pious will ride any vehicle that is going their way.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Dancer

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Dancing Master

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Fiddler

snapshots.name: The Dogmatist

snapshots.name: The Idealist
snapshots.body: Whose fantasy is tyrannical tonight, so that if all this is himself, he is a fool.

snapshots.name: God
snapshots.body: Named throughout by Faust, Margaret and Mephistopheles alike; in the Prologue he speaks as the Lord.

snapshots.body: Risen in the Easter chorus that stops Faust’s hand on the poison cup.

snapshots.name: Satan

snapshots.name: Solomon
snapshots.body: Whose key the Witch’s nonsense book parodies.

snapshots.name: The Chorus of Angels
snapshots.body: The Easter choir that sings Christ is arisen — which does not convert Faust but does keep him alive.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Chorus of Spirits
snapshots.body: Mephistopheles’s invisible servants, who tell Faust he has smashed the world and invite him to build it again.

snapshots.name: The Voice from Above
snapshots.body: The last word of the play: Mephistopheles says Margaret is judged, and the voice says she is saved.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Faust
snapshots.body: The scholar who has read everything and knows nothing worth knowing, and signs away his soul for one moment he would want to keep. The wager is his own idea, and so is its wording.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mephistopheles
snapshots.body: The devil who bets the Lord that he can have Faust, and then finds that ruining him is harder than it looked. He calls himself the spirit that always denies, and he is the funniest thing in the play.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Martha
snapshots.body: Margaret’s neighbour, a widow who is not much troubled about her missing husband and is very ready to be courted by Mephistopheles.

snapshots.name: Wagner
snapshots.body: Faust’s assistant, entirely content with books and eager to be told he is making progress. Goethe uses him to show what Faust might have settled for.

snapshots.name: The Student
snapshots.body: The freshman who comes for advice and is sent off by Mephistopheles, in Faust’s gown, with a course of study designed to ruin him — and an autograph that reads "you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil."

snapshots.name: The Poodle
snapshots.body: The black dog that follows Faust home from the walk and turns out to be the devil; Faust spends a whole scene talking to it before it changes shape.

snapshots.name: Nostradamus
snapshots.body: The astrologer whose book of signs Faust opens, and in which he finds the sign of the Macrocosm and then the sign of the Earth Spirit.

snapshots.name: Frosch
snapshots.body: One of the four drinkers in Auerbach’s Cellar, and the one who tries hardest to keep the party going.

snapshots.name: Brander

snapshots.name: Siebel
snapshots.body: A drinker in Auerbach’s Cellar, unlucky in love and the first to grab for Mephistopheles’s throat.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Altmayer

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Witch
snapshots.body: The keeper of the kitchen where Faust is made thirty years younger; she recognises Mephistopheles at once and is scolded for using his old names.

snapshots.name: The Monkeys
snapshots.body: The witch’s household, who mind the cauldron, play with a crown and a glass ball, and beg for money.

snapshots.name: Helen

snapshots.name: Raphael
snapshots.body: The first of the three archangels in the Prologue in Heaven, who sings of the sun and its brother spheres.

snapshots.name: Gabriel

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Michael

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Three
snapshots.body: The archangels singing together, closing the Prologue’s hymn before Mephistopheles speaks.

snapshots.name: The Manager
snapshots.body: In the Prelude on the Stage, the one who wants a full house and tells the Poet what an audience actually is.

snapshots.name: The Poet
snapshots.body: In the Prelude, the one who refuses to write for the crowd and is told he will have to.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Merryman
snapshots.body: In the Prelude, the comic actor, who sides with neither and tells them both to get on with it.

snapshots.name: The townsfolk at the gate
snapshots.body: Goethe’s crowd on Easter Sunday, speaking in anonymous voices — mechanics choosing a tavern, servant-girls, burghers glad of a war far away in Turkey, a beggar, a soldier, a citizen’s daughter warned off the fortune-teller. None of them is named, and that is the point: this is the world Faust cannot be content with.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Old Peasant
snapshots.body: The villager who brings Faust the first draught, because Faust’s father worked among them in the plague year — the thanks that makes Faust confess what his father’s medicine actually did.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Faust’s father
snapshots.body: The dark man of honour who brewed the red lion and the lily in his laboratory and killed more patients than the plague; Faust says so while accepting their gratitude.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Luther
snapshots.body: Named only for his paunch, in Brander’s song about the rat.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Mr Hans of Rippach
snapshots.body: A stock joke — the man from Rippach who does not exist, whom Mephistopheles is asked whether he supped with.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Jack Rake
snapshots.body: The name Margaret’s type of admirer is given: a man who covets every flower for himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Will-o’-the-Wisp
snapshots.body: The zigzag light pressed into service as a guide up the Brocken, and told to go straight for once.

snapshots.name: Lilith
snapshots.body: Adam’s first wife, dancing on the Brocken; Mephistopheles warns Faust about her beautiful hair.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Squire Voland
snapshots.body: The old German name for the devil, which Mephistopheles uses to clear a path through the crowd on the mountain.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The General
snapshots.body: One of four has-beens sitting by the dying embers on the Brocken, complaining that the world has passed him by.

snapshots.name: The Minister
snapshots.body: A second of the four by the embers, who remembers when merit still counted.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Fair One
snapshots.body: The young witch Faust dances with, whose song about the apple tree he answers in kind.

snapshots.body: The old witch who dances with Mephistopheles and matches his coarseness.

snapshots.name: The Proktophantasmist
snapshots.body: Goethe’s caricature of a living critic who denied ghosts in print; he turns up on a mountain full of them and complains that they will not obey the rules.

snapshots.name: Servibilis
snapshots.body: The busybody who announces the amateur theatricals about to begin — the Walpurgis-Night’s Dream.

snapshots.name: Medusa
snapshots.body: Whose name Mephistopheles gives to the pale girl Faust cannot look away from — the vision with a red thread round her throat.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Perseus
snapshots.body: Named for having cut off the head the vision carries under her arm.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: The Demi-Witch
snapshots.body: One of the crowd toiling up the mountain, a hundred years behind the others.

snapshots.name: The Chorus of Witches
snapshots.body: The crowd streaming to the summit — the salve gives courage, a rag serves for a sail.

snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed ordinary identity for recognition; trigger is not a claim that every identity fact precedes the selected name.

snapshots.name: Oberon

snapshots.name: The Spirit that is Fashioning Itself
snapshots.body: A half-made creature in the masque, all legs and no body yet.

snapshots.body: Whose key the Witch’s nonsense book parodies.

snapshots.name: The Chorus of Angels

snapshots.name: The Chorus of Spirits
snapshots.body: Mephistopheles’s invisible servants, who tell Faust he has smashed the world and invite him to build it again.

snapshots.name: The Voice from Above
snapshots.body: The last word of the play: Mephistopheles says Margaret is judged, and the voice says she is saved.
